evidence.snippet:
referred to as “mortar” and “paste,” respectively.
The specific preparation and curing procedures for AAM mortar were 
as follows. First, the precursors, aggregates, and a solid activator were 
placed in a planetary mixer and dry-mixed at 75 r/min for 3 min to 
ensure uniformity. Then, tap water was added, and mixing continued for 
another 3 min to obtain a homogeneous paste. The fresh paste was cast 
into molds and compacted on a vibration table. After the initial setting, 
the specimens were covered with plastic film and cured under labora­
tory conditions for 24 h. After demolding, the specimens were cured 
under standard conditions until the testing ages of 3, 7, and 28 days for 
mechanical property evaluation.
The prepared specimens consisted of 50 mm × 50 mm × 50 mm
cubes for compressive strength tests and 40 mm  40 mm  160 mm

as follows. First, the precursors, aggregates, and a solid activator were 
placed in a planetary mixer and dry-mixed at 75 r/min for 3 min to 
ensure uniformity. Then, tap water was added, and mixing continued for 
another 3 min to obtain a homogeneous paste. The fresh paste was cast 
into molds and compacted on a vibration table. After the initial setting, 
the specimens were covered with plastic film and cured under labora­
tory conditions for 24 h. After demolding, the specimens were cured 
under standard conditions until the testing ages of 3, 7, and 28 days for 
mechanical property evaluation.

The mixing method of AAFS concrete is presented as follows. FA, GGBS, fine
aggregate and coarse aggregate were dry-mixed for 2 min to ensure homogeneity
of the mixture. Then, AL and SPs were added into mixture and mixed for another
3 min. The fresh AAFS concrete was then immediately cast into three different
moulds (cube with size of 100 mm for compressive test, cylinder with size of
100 �200 mm for splitting tensile test and prism with size of 100 �100�500
mm for four-point bending test and dynamic elastic modulus test). For each testing
age, three specimens were prepared for each mixture. All specimens were then
stored in a curing room (20 ± 2 �C, 60% ± 5% RH). After 24 h, the specimens were
de-moulded and placed in curing room under the same environmental condition
until the day of testing.

aggregate and coarse aggregate were dry-mixed for 2 min to ensure homogeneity
of the mixture. Then, AL and SPs were added into mixture and mixed for another
3 min. The fresh AAFS concrete was then immediately cast into three different
moulds (cube with size of 100 mm for compressive test, cylinder with size of
100 �200 mm for splitting tensile test and prism with size of 100 �100�500
mm for four-point bending test and dynamic elastic modulus test). For each testing
age, three specimens were prepared for each mixture. All specimens were then
stored in a curing room (20 ± 2 �C, 60% ± 5% RH). After 24 h, the specimens were
de-moulded and placed in curing room under the same environmental condition
until the day of testing.

the viscosity of the freshly prepared paste was measured (step 2). The 
paste was divided into two portions; one part was poured into the open 
mold placed in a sealed plastic bag, whereas the other part was placed in 
an air-tight plastic tube (step 3). Both subsamples were cured in an oven 
(Type TS 8056, Termaks, Bergen, Norway) at 60 ◦C for 24 h (step 4). The 
cured samples were cut in half (step 5), and the subsamples (plate and 
tube) were cured in an oven (Modell 600. Memmert GmbH+Co.KG 
Schwabach. Germany) at 105 ◦C for 72 h (step 6). This preparation 
process yields four types of AAM: (a) AAM open plate-mold 60 ◦C, (b) 
AAM sealed tube-mold 60 ◦C, (c) AAM open plate-mold 105 ◦C, and (d) 
AAM sealed tube-mold 105 ◦C. 
All samples were weighed to determine the moisture lost during the 
curing process. The volume of the paste in the air-tight sealed plastic

evidence.snippet:
60 strokes on a Proeti shaking table to eliminate air bubbles and enhance 
compaction. The specimens were then cured at 60 ◦C for 72 h while 
wrapped in an adhesive film. This temperature is in the range of con­
ditions reviewed for curing geopolymers [62]. After the 72 h period, the 
samples were removed from the molds and kept at room temperature 
until the characterization tests were conducted at 7 and 28 days. For 
each mixture, 24 rectangular specimens were fabricated. These samples
were labeled as x-CDW-y, where x denotes the CDW content (100, 80, or 
60 wt%, with the remainder being RHA), and y indicates the activator 
modulus, Ms (0.5, 1.0, 2.0).

The sample preparation methodology is outlined as follows. Initially, the solid raw materials were introduced into the mixing pot 
and dry-mixed at a slow rate for 90 s until a homogeneous blend was obtained. Subsequently, the alkali activator and additional water 
were added, and the mixture was gently stirred for 90 s to form a uniform slurry. The material adhering to the bottom of the mixing pot 
was then scraped using a putty knife for 30 s while the mixer was paused to ensure complete mixing. Finally, the slurry was mixed at 
high speed for an additional 90 s to achieve full homogeneity. The fresh paste was cast into 40 mm × 40 mm × 160 mm molds in two 
layers and compacted by vibration for 60 s to remove entrapped air. The surface was leveled and covered with plastic film to prevent 
moisture loss. Specimens were demolded after 24 h of curing at room temperature and then transferred to a standard curing chamber 
until the specified testing ages. The curing conditions were 20 ± 2 ◦C and relative humidity of 95%.

evidence.snippet:
was introduced into the dry mixed precursors to prepare the AAB slurry 
paste. The wet mixing was carried out for 10 min until homogenous 
mixture with good workability was obtained. Fresh AAB pastes were 
transferred into molds of 40 × 40 × 40 mm3 size. The fresh pastes were 
placed on a vibrator to remove air bubbles and for compaction purpose. 
The molds were then wrapped with plastic sheets and were placed in an 
electric oven at a fixed temperature of 80 ◦C for 72 h. It is important to 
mention that the reactivity of FGR based activator is very low at the 
ambient conditions so heat curing was adopted to obtain the AABs 
having high strength. After 3 days of heat curing, samples were cooled 
down to ambient temperature in oven for 24 h, demolded and tested for 
compressive strength and microstructural properties.

tween the two binders: 100 % slag and 50 % slag-50 % fly ash.
Paste specimens were cast into cylindrical silicon molds with a
diameter of 25 mm (1 in.) and a height of 12.5 mm (0.5 in.). Initial
curing was carried out for a duration of 28 days at a temperature of 24 ±
2 ◦C and a relative humidity (RH) of 95 ± 2 %. These conditions were
chosen to maximize the hydration and to minimize the occurrence of
carbonation. It is well-known that high moisture content can signifi-
cantly slow down the carbonation process as the diffusion coefficient of
CO2 is significantly lower in the aqueous state compared to the gas state.
After the initial curing, paste specimens were crushed using a mortar
and pestle. Then, the pulverized paste specimens were filtered by
sieving, where the collected specimens passed sieve No. 16 (1.18 mm)
and retained on sieve No. 30 (600 μm). This sample preparation was
conducted to achieve a homogeneous surface area and a uniform CO2
ingress during the carbonation stage. An optical microscope image of the
pulverized paste particles is shown in Fig. 3.

2.3. CO2 curing procedure
In this study, CO2 curing was conducted in an incubator under
controlled conditions, with a CO2 concentration of 1 ± 0.1 %, a tem-
perature of 24 ± 2 ◦C, a relative humidity (RH) of 65 ± 2 %, and under
atmospheric pressure. The selection of the CO2 concentration aimed to
achieve a low carbonate/calcium ratio in the pore solution. Each binder
underwent curing for three different durations: 0, 28, and 56 days. It
should be noted that the specimens undergoing 0-day CO2 curing were
carefully stored in a controlled chamber with a temperature maintained
at 24 ± 2 ◦C and a relative humidity (RH) of 95 ± 2 %. Table 4 provides
a list of the studied binders, categorized based on their composition and
curing stage.

controlled conditions, with a CO2 concentration of 1 ± 0.1 %, a tem-

achieve a low carbonate/calcium ratio in the pore solution. Each binder
underwent curing for three different durations: 0, 28, and 56 days. It
should be noted that the specimens undergoing 0-day CO2 curing were
